notes.front: Who can remove a restrictive legend from a securities certificate?
notes.back: Only a transfer agent, and only with the issuer’s consent, usually given as an opinion letter from the issuer’s counsel.
notes.explanation: Even after meeting Rule 144, restricted securities cannot be sold publicly until the legend is removed.
notes.evidence: Only a transfer agent can remove a restrictive legend. But the transfer agent won't remove the legend unless the issuer consents—usually in the form of an opinion letter from the issuer's counsel to the transfer agent.

notes.front: What does SEC Rule 144 permit?
notes.back: Public resale of restricted or control securities, if conditions on holding period, manner of sale and amount are met.
notes.explanation: Rule 144 is the most commonly used exemption for selling restricted securities.
notes.evidence: Rule 144 provides an exemption and permits the public resale of restricted or control securities if a number of conditions are met, including how long the securities are held, the way in which they are sold, and the amount that can be sold at any one time.

notes.front: Under Rule 144, who is an affiliate of an issuer?
notes.back: A person who controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with the issuer, directly or indirectly.
notes.explanation: Affiliates face extra limits on their sales under Rule 144.
notes.evidence: (1) An affiliate of an issuer is a person that directly, or indirectly through one or more intermediaries, controls, or is controlled by, or is under common control with, such issuer.

notes.front: Under Rule 144, do an affiliate’s volume limits apply only to restricted securities?
notes.back: No. They apply to an affiliate’s sales whether or not the securities are restricted.
notes.explanation: Restrictions attach to how the securities were acquired; affiliate limits attach to who is selling.
notes.evidence: (1) If any securities are sold for the account of an affiliate of the issuer, regardless of whether those securities are restricted, the amount of securities sold, together with all sales of securities of the same class sold for the account of such person within the preceding three months, shall not exceed the greatest of:

notes.front: Under Rule 144, what is the minimum holding period for restricted securities of an issuer that has been a reporting company for at least 90 days?
notes.back: Six months.
notes.explanation: An issuer counts here only once it has been subject to Exchange Act reporting for at least 90 days.
notes.evidence: (i) If the issuer of the securities is, and has been for a period of at least 90 days immediately before the sale, subject to the reporting requirements of section 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act, a minimum of six months must elapse

notes.front: Under Rule 144, what is the minimum holding period for restricted securities of a non-reporting issuer?
notes.back: One year.
notes.explanation: It applies when the issuer is not, or has not been for at least 90 days, subject to Exchange Act reporting.
notes.evidence: (ii) If the issuer of the securities is not, or has not been for a period of at least 90 days immediately before the sale, subject to the reporting requirements of section 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act, a minimum of one year must elapse

notes.front: An investor bought restricted shares from a private company that files no SEC reports. Seven months later, may she resell under Rule 144?
notes.back: Not yet: for a non-reporting issuer the holding period is one year.
notes.explanation: The six-month period applies only to issuers that have been reporting for at least 90 days.
notes.evidence: (ii) If the issuer of the securities is not, or has not been for a period of at least 90 days immediately before the sale, subject to the reporting requirements of section 13 or 15(d) of the Exchange Act, a minimum of one year must elapse

notes.front: Under Rule 144, what is one measure in the affiliate volume limit, based on shares outstanding?
notes.back: 1% of the shares of the class outstanding.
notes.explanation: The limit is the greatest of this and the trading-volume measures, over any three months.
notes.evidence: (i) One percent of the shares or other units of the class outstanding as shown by the most recent report or statement published by the issuer, or

notes.front: Under Rule 144, what trading-volume measure can set an affiliate’s volume limit?
notes.back: The average weekly reported trading volume over the four calendar weeks before the Form 144 notice.
notes.explanation: The affiliate may sell up to the greatest of this and 1% of shares outstanding.
notes.evidence: (ii) The average weekly reported volume of trading in such securities on all national securities exchanges and/or reported through the automated quotation system of a registered securities association during the four calendar weeks preceding the filing of notice

notes.front: An affiliate’s company has 20 million shares outstanding and average weekly volume of 150,000 over the last four weeks. What is the most she can sell in three months under Rule 144?
notes.back: 200,000 shares: the greater of 1% of outstanding (200,000) and weekly volume (150,000).
notes.explanation: Rule 144 takes the greatest of its measures, not the smallest.
notes.evidence: the amount of securities sold, together with all sales of securities of the same class sold for the account of such person within the preceding three months, shall not exceed the greatest of:

notes.front: An affiliate plans to sell 3,000 shares worth $40,000 under Rule 144 this quarter. Must she file Form 144?
notes.back: No. Form 144 is needed only above 5,000 shares or $50,000 in any three months.
notes.explanation: Her sale is under both thresholds.
notes.evidence: the amount of securities to be sold in reliance upon this rule during any period of three months exceeds 5,000 shares or other units or has an aggregate sale price in excess of $50,000, a notice on Form 144

notes.front: Under Rule 144A, to whom may the securities be sold?
notes.back: Only to qualified institutional buyers, or to buyers the seller reasonably believes are.
notes.explanation: Rule 144A gives the seller non-exclusive ways to check a buyer’s status, such as recent financial statements.
notes.evidence: (1) The securities are sold only to a qualified institutional buyer or to a purchaser that the seller and any person acting on behalf of the seller reasonably believe is a qualified institutional buyer.

notes.front: An individual with $30 million invested in securities wants to buy in a Rule 144A offering. Is he a qualified institutional buyer?
notes.back: No. Rule 144A’s categories are entities, such as institutions and registered dealers, not individuals.
notes.explanation: Being wealthy can make someone an accredited investor, but QIB status is for listed entity types.
notes.evidence: (i) Any of the following entities, acting for its own account or the accounts of other qualified institutional buyers, that in the aggregate owns and invests on a discretionary basis at least $100 million in securities of issuers that are not affiliated with the entity:

notes.front: What is SEC Rule 145 designed to do?
notes.back: Extend the protection of Securities Act registration to people offered securities in business combinations it describes.
notes.explanation: Its transactions are treated as involving an offer or sale of securities to the security holders who vote on them.
notes.evidence: Rule 145 (§ 230.145 of this chapter) is designed to make available the protection provided by registration under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (Act), to persons who are offered securities in a business combination

notes.front: Under Rule 147, where is a corporate issuer deemed resident?
notes.back: In the state where it is incorporated or organised and has its principal place of business.
notes.explanation: The principal place of business is where its officers primarily direct, control and coordinate its activities.
notes.evidence: (i) It is incorporated or organized, and it has its principal place of business, if a corporation, limited partnership, trust or other form of business organization that is organized under state or territorial law.

notes.front: Under Rule 147, how many of the “doing business” tests must an issuer meet?
notes.back: At least one.
notes.explanation: The tests include 80% of revenues, 80% of net proceeds used in-state, or a majority of employees based there.
notes.evidence: (2) The issuer shall be deemed to be doing business within a state or territory if the issuer satisfies at least one of the following requirements:

notes.front: A Florida-incorporated firm run from Miami earns most revenue out of state but has most of its staff in Florida. Can it meet Rule 147’s doing-business requirement?
notes.back: Yes: having a majority of its employees based in the state is one of the qualifying tests.
notes.explanation: Only one of the doing-business tests needs to be met.
notes.evidence: (iv) A majority of the issuer's employees are based in such state or territory.

notes.front: Under Rule 147, to whom may the offers and sales be made?
notes.back: Only to residents of the issuer’s state, or people the issuer reasonably believes are residents.
notes.explanation: The whole offering must stay within that state.
notes.evidence: Offers and sales of securities pursuant to this section (§ 230.147) shall be made only to residents of the state or territory in which the issuer is resident

notes.front: Four months after buying in a Texas company’s Rule 147 offering, a Texas resident wants to sell his shares to a buyer in New Mexico. May he?
notes.back: No. For six months after the issuer’s sale, resales may be made only to residents of the issuer’s state.
notes.explanation: The resale limit keeps the offering within the state for its first six months.
notes.evidence: For a period of six months from the date of the sale by the issuer of a security pursuant to this section (§ 230.147), any resale of such security shall be made only to persons resident within the state or territory in which the issuer was resident

notes.front: Under section 15(a) of the Exchange Act, what must a broker or dealer generally be before using interstate commerce to effect securities transactions?
notes.back: Registered with the SEC under section 15(b).
notes.explanation: The section makes it unlawful to trade non-exempt securities otherwise, with narrow exceptions such as purely intrastate businesses.
notes.evidence: unless such broker or dealer is registered in accordance with subsection (b) of this section.

notes.front: Under section 15A of the Exchange Act, what may an association of brokers and dealers register as?
notes.back: A national securities association (or an affiliated securities association).
notes.explanation: A registered securities association is one of the kinds of SRO the Act recognises.
notes.evidence: An association of brokers and dealers may be registered as a national securities association

notes.front: What are two kinds of financial instrument that CUSIP numbers identify?
notes.back: Any two of: stocks of registered American and Canadian companies; commercial paper; federal government bonds; municipal bonds.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov says CUSIP numbers identify most financial instruments.
notes.evidence: A CUSIP number identifies most financial instruments, including: stocks of all registered U.S. and Canadian companies, commercial paper, and U.S. government and municipal bonds.
